body: The roundabout has four exits and he takes the third, which puts him on the ring road and adds eleven minutes to the drive. He has done that since March. The direct way goes past a shop with a car park he knows the shape of, and this is a Tuesday at ten past four with the job finished early, which is exactly the sort of Tuesday it is worth adding eleven minutes to. He turns the radio up because the ring road is dull. He gets in at the usual time. His wife asks whether the traffic was bad and he says it was fine. That is the entire event.

Nothing happened. Nobody knows anything happened. There is no version of that afternoon that anybody would stand up and describe, and it is the only part of the whole business that is actually load-bearing.
Church culture loves a recovery testimony, and there is a good reason for it: it has a shape. Bondage, intervention, freedom. Somebody stands at the front, tells it in the past tense, and it ends.

The shape is the problem, and it is worth being precise about why. A testimony is a story, and a story is a thing with an arc that resolves — which makes it tellable, memorable and moving, and makes it a very poor map of the terrain it claims to describe. What is being described is not an event. It is a practice with no terminal point, conducted mostly in private, in which the decisive moments are unremarkable: a Tuesday afternoon, a familiar route not taken, a phone call made before rather than after, an early night on the evening everybody else stayed. Nobody is going to ask a man to come and speak about a roundabout.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air. Two frequencies are assigned to this subject and are still in build — HM 391.20, Freedom Steps, and HM 391.50, Strong Sober — and nothing plays on either of them yet.

Programming for that is unrewarding work and it is the reason those two are taking their time. There is no arc to build an hour around. Nothing on such a frequency can be climactic, because a climax is precisely the lie being corrected, and nothing on it can congratulate anybody, because congratulation is the sound support makes just before it leaves. What is left is showing up at the same time and being ordinary, day after day, at some length. It is worth doing for one reason. A testimony has an ending. Recovery does not, and the mismatch between those two shapes does real damage.

The damage runs in both directions. To the person, it teaches that the interesting part of their life was the worst part of it, and that everything since — which is the actual achievement, and cost more — is filler between the good bit and now. To everybody else it teaches that the matter is closed. The story reached its ending, the room applauded, and the calls and the invitations tail off over the following months, at exactly the point where nothing external is happening any more and the whole thing has become a private matter of getting through Tuesday.

The band is arranged so that a listener can find a register without hunting for it. The online church and recovery frequencies sit together in their own stretch rather than being scattered through the music, so a person who wants that corner of the dial can put a hand on it. Several of them are held and still in build, which is deliberate: an empty frequency is better than a filled one that is wrong, and this is a subject where wrong does harm. Learn roughly where things sit and you can move about without looking.
None of which is an argument against telling the story. It is an argument about what happens on the Thursday after you told it.

Be fair to the testimony first, because it does work nothing else does. It tells a person still in it that the thing is survivable, which is not obvious from inside and cannot be established by argument. It breaks shame in a room, publicly, in a way no leaflet can. Somebody standing up and saying it out loud has often been the moment another person in the fourth row decided to make a phone call. But a story cannot be present. It happened once, it is finished, and its shape teaches the audience that this sort of thing concludes — so support arrives in a rush at the dramatic part and thins out over the part that lasts the rest of a life.
The story is over by Sunday evening. Tuesday is not.

A woman of about fifty is at her daughter’s wedding, standing near the top table while the toasts are being done. She has an orange juice in a proper glass, which the staff sorted out earlier without being asked twice, and she holds it up with everybody else. That part is fine. What is not fine is twenty minutes later, when the room has gone loose and loud and nobody needs her for anything, and she goes out into the corridor by the coats and stands there. A radio is on through the door to the kitchens, playing something with too much energy for a corridor. She stays where she is until it has finished, which is about three minutes. Then she goes back in and dances with her brother.
Nothing happened in that corridor either. It was the hardest part of her daughter’s wedding and there is no way to tell it that makes it a story.

It has to be said plainly what a station cannot do. It cannot hold anybody accountable, notice a relapse, ring anybody, or know your name. Music has never got a single person sober and never will. Nothing here substitutes for a doctor, for a room with other people in it who have the same problem, or for the person you are supposed to phone. And this article will not tell you that the Tuesdays get easier on any particular schedule, because for some people they do and for some they do not, and anybody offering a timetable is selling something.

That refusal to promise is not a weakness in the format. It is the whole of its usefulness. Everything else aimed at this subject promises: a programme, a breakthrough, a number of days, a moment when it lifts. A frequency makes one commitment, which is that it will be at the same number tomorrow, playing whether or not you are having a good day and whether or not you deserve it. That is the identical shape of the thing being asked of the listener — do it again, on time, regardless of how you feel — and it is the only shape that does not quietly imply an end date.

So the flat Tuesday is not the gap between testimonies. It is the thing itself, and the story, if there ever is one, is a souvenir of the beginning of it. What a person in that position needs from a room, or from a radio, is not admiration for the past tense. It is company in the present one: something running at four in the afternoon that started before they tuned in, will still be going when they arrive home, and has no idea whether this is day nine or year nine.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial, and it is worth knowing they are there before you turn it. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a great deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them. No menu, no queue, nothing to decide before anything starts.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 302.50 — Pentecostal Shout. It is on air, and it is louder than you are going to feel on a Tuesday afternoon, which is the point of recommending it. It is not matching your mood and it is not trying to. It is a room that was already going before you got there, from a tradition whose instinct is that praise is a thing you do out loud and repeatedly rather than when you happen to be moved — which is this article’s argument about the four o’clock drive home, sung. Nobody on it will ask what day you are on.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people reach for, which is how the next one gets built and how a frequency like Freedom Steps gets its turn.

So take this as an invitation rather than a plan, because a plan is one more thing to fail at by Friday. Put HM 302.50 on tomorrow at whatever hour is your worst one and leave it running while you do something with your hands. It will not fix the hour. Nothing does. But the hour will pass with a room in it that is going on regardless, and then it will be Wednesday, and you can do the same thing again — which is, as far as anybody has ever been able to establish, the whole method.
